memories.content: Avoid em dashes in the proposal; split the sentence or use more ordinary punctuation instead.
The user tends to place several independently reviewable claims in one long sentence.
Use first-person active voice for choices and commitments owned by the proposal author so responsibility remains explicit throughout the work plan.
Describe prototype operations that have already been implemented and verified as observed states.
Describe prototype operations not yet implemented or evaluated as plans or expectations.
When a commitment is phrased passively, readers may interpret it as uncertainty, evasiveness, or reluctance to take responsibility.
Use “we” only for decisions and commitments the authors control, not for external facts or actions owned by another party.
The user should use one first-person pronoun consistently for the same authorial role and should not alternate between “I” and “we” unless the responsible party actually changes.
The user tends to hide unsettled commitments behind passive phrases such as “will be considered” or “is expected.”
Split proposal prose into short sentences when a sentence contains more than one independently reviewable claim.
Keep one main claim in each sentence so a reviewer can locate and assess it quickly.
The user tends to repeat em dashes when a sentence already contains several clauses.
Repeated em dashes can shift a reviewer’s attention from the proposal’s argument to suspicion that its prose was generated by AI.
Do not exceed two primary HCI contributions that readers must remember.
Present each design or operational contribution as a single named sentence.
In studies recruiting organizational members, emphasize workflow constraints.
In studies recruiting organizational members, emphasize manager approval constraints.
HCI reviewers find it difficult to identify primary contributions when named design and operational contributions exceed two.
Highlight one primary field operational decision to be changed by evaluation results as the central claim.
Specify prototype features unnecessary for reviewing the primary field problem as secondary scope.

analysis.overview: The frames converge only on sentence-level clarity, with the compared guidance narrowing that principle to named contributions. Otherwise, the reference emphasizes voice, tense, punctuation, and claim separation, while the compared frame governs contribution limits, field-study framing, central decisions, and secondary feature scope.

relations.reason: The reference identifies and corrects multi-claim sentences generally; the compared guidance preserves that principle within an explicit contribution-specific scope.
relations.summary: Both frames promote sentence-level isolation of reviewable claims, while the compared frame applies the rule specifically to named design or operational contributions.

reports.compared_only: Compared-only guidance limits memorable HCI contributions, foregrounds organizational constraints and one evaluation-sensitive field decision, and marks nonessential prototype features as secondary.
reports.differences: Sentence-level claim separation in the reference becomes a contribution-specific naming rule in the compared frame.
reports.reference_only: Reference-only guidance covers em dashes, active authorial responsibility, pronoun ownership and consistency, passive commitments, and evidence-sensitive prototype tense.
